To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the energy cost of steady state physical activity in acute stroke is high, and that the energy cost for a given activity decreases as the patient recovers.
the energy cost of steady state physical activity in acute stroke is 1.5 times higher than that in healthy individuals.
the energy cost of walking is higher in stroke survivors than in age-matched controls, but that this difference is eliminated with a cane and is further diminished by a walker.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the energy cost of steady state physical activity (i.e. walking) in patients with acute stroke.
the energy cost of steady-state physical activity in patients with stroke and its relation to functional status.
the energy cost of walking and the effects of physical activity in acute stroke patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the energy cost of walking is higher in patients with acute stroke than in healthy individuals.
, in general, there is a significant reduction of the energy cost of walking in patients with stroke.
the energy cost of physical activity in acute stroke is high.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a new method for measuring the energy cost of physical activity in acute stroke.
the energy cost of walking in stroke patients is higher and more variable than that of age-matched healthy controls.
the energy expenditure of steady state physical activity is higher in the first 3 months following acute stroke than in the chronic phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cost of steady state physical activity is higher in acute stroke compared to healthy controls.
the cost of physical activity is not constant and varies depending on how much activity is performed and how long it is performed.
stroke survivors are capable of achieving high levels of physical activity.
